{{nihongo|'''Shizuma Shrine'''|静間神社}} is a [[shinto shrine]] in the [[Engishiki Jinmyōchō]]. It is located in [[Iwami Province]].

=== Explanation ===
It was founded in {{ill|Ninna|Q1346317|qid=Q1346317}} 2 (886), and the current main sanctuary is built in Kasuga-zukuri style.

The main deities are {{ill|Ōkuninushi|abstract|Q276944|ca|Ōkuninushi|es|Ōkuninushi|fa|اوکونینوشی|fr|Ōkuninushi|hu|Ókuninusi|id|Ookuninushi|it|Ōkuninushi|ja|大国主|ko|오오쿠니누시|mni|ꯑꯣꯀꯨꯅꯤꯅꯨꯁꯤ|pl|Ōkuninushi|pt|Ookuninushi|ru|Окунинуси|simple|Ōkuninushi|sr|Okuninuši|sv|Ōkuninushi|tr|Ōkuninushi|uk|Окунінуші|vi|Ōkuninushi|zh|大國主|qid=Q276944|lt=Ōnamuchi-no-Mikoto}} and {{ill|Sukunabikona|ca|Sukunabikona|fr|Sukunabikona|it|Sukuna-hikona|ja|スクナビコナ|ko|스쿠나비코나|mni|ꯁꯨꯀꯨꯅꯕꯤꯀꯣꯅ|pl|Sukunabikona|pt|Sukunahikona|simple|Sukunabikona|sv|Suku-Na-Bikona|zh|少彥名|qid=Q3275687|lt=Sukunahikona-no-Mikoto}}. Since the {{ill|Meiji era|Q3125096|qid=Q3125096}} period, two Hachimangū shrines, two Itsukushima shrines, Ōtoshi Shrine, Kareki Shrine, and others formerly in the village have been merged and enshrined in the main sanctuary.

As precinct shrines, there is Tenmangū on the left (formerly Tarumi Hachimangū, but after merger with Kami-Shizuma Hachimangū and transfer to the main sanctuary, it now enshrines the Tenjin deity that had stood before the waterfall); on the right is Tōshōgū (because it was former {{ill|Tenryō|Q1685411|qid=Q1685411}}, it enshrines {{ill|Tokugawa Ieyasu|Q171977|qid=Q171977}} and {{ill|Mōri Terumoto|Q1142657|qid=Q1142657}}); and in the pond is Suijin Shrine (formerly Ukanomitama Shrine, with {{ill|Ukanomitama|lt=Ukanomitama|Q3080728|qid=Q3080728|qid=Q3080728|lt=Ukanomitama}} as deity, now enshrined in the main sanctuary; an Itsukushima Shrine is also presumed to have been here). The {{ill|Reisai|Q11385469|qid=Q11385469}} is April 15 (until the Meiji period, it was on the 15th days of the 3rd and 9th lunar months).

At the time of foundation, the shrine was enshrined inside {{ill|Shizu no Iwaya|Q11662872|qid=Q11662872}}, associated with the Man'yōshū, in the nearby Uozu settlement. After damage from high waves, it once moved outside the cave, then a heavy rain in June {{ill|1674|Q7620|qid=Q7620}} ({{ill|Enpō|Q1145735|qid=Q1145735}} 2) caused a debris-flow mountain tsunami that collapsed the shrine building, so it was moved to Mount Tarumi the following year.

The shrine preserves as many as 104 munafuda dating from 1650 onward. These plaques show that even in the {{ill|Edo period|Q184963|qid=Q184963}}, when commoners were not permitted {{ill|myoujitaitou|Q11616116|qid=Q11616116|lt=surnames and sword-bearing}}, residents used {{ill|myōji|Q69634220|qid=Q69634220|lt=surnames}} in shrine activities and lived actively.
